title: Herdr publishes a paid tier above its Apache-2.0 runtime by Q2 2027
body:
Herdr said on Thursday, August 6 that it has joined Y Combinator's F26 batch, and in the same post it relicensed its runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0. Herdr is a terminal runtime for command-line coding agents: it organises them into panes, tabs and projects and keeps them running persistently on the machine they sit on, and those machines are disconnected from each other today. No funding figure appears anywhere in the announcement, and a batch admission is not a round, so there is no number attached to this and none should be inferred. What the post does state is a split. The runtime people use today stays free under Apache-2.0, and commercial features get built on top of it, with multi-machine connectivity and clients beyond the terminal interface named as the two candidates.

The licence line is the load-bearing one, and it is worth being exact about what moved. AGPL's network-use clause is what would have obliged a hosted service built on Herdr to publish its own source; Apache-2.0 removes that obligation. From the outside that reads as an adoption change - a company that could not put an AGPL runtime behind its own service now can. From the inside it is the opposite of a moat. The clause that just came out was the one thing in the stack reserving the hosted layer for the people who wrote the runtime, and giving it up leaves that layer reserved by nothing except being first and being better. A company that drops its legal claim on the layer it has said it intends to sell has a reason to turn that layer into a priced product rather than a stated plan, because the licence is no longer holding the position for it.

The same week supplies the pressure from the other side. Meta's research group published Muse Code on Wednesday, August 5, a terminal coding agent explicitly in beta, whose subagents persist for the whole session rather than being spawned per task and whose every model call, tool run, approval and edit is appended to a local event log that makes a run replay-exact and restart-safe. Persistence across a session and survival across a restart are the same concerns Herdr's runtime advertises, and the announcement names no price for any of it. That does not make the two substitutes - Muse Code is an agent, Herdr is the runtime other agents run inside - but it does show which way capability travels in this layer once a large research group decides to ship it, and it is an argument against the runtime itself ever being the thing that carries a bill.

The prediction is that the intent becomes a number. By the end of Q2 2027, Herdr publishes a price for a paid tier of its own - a plan or pricing page, or an equivalent published document stating what the tier costs - and the description of that tier names at least one of the two things the August 6 post identified as commercial: connectivity across multiple machines, or a client beyond the terminal interface. The runtime remaining available under Apache-2.0 alongside it is expected rather than a complication; that is the split the post described.

Several near misses do not count, and each is what a company at this stage reaches for first. A waitlist, an early-access form or a coming-soon banner does not count, because the claim is about a published price and not about a published intention. Restating the August 6 plan in a later post does not count for the same reason. A sponsorship or donation button does not count: that is a way of paying maintainers, not a price on a layer. An enterprise page inviting the reader to contact sales, carrying no figure, does not count. A free hosted service does not count until it carries a price, however plainly it is the eventual paid thing. And a funding announcement does not count in either direction - a round is not a price, and the batch admission that prompted this was not a round.

Two objections are worth stating plainly. The first is that nothing in the source sets a clock. The post names the commercial candidates, gives no date for them and no figure for anything, and a small team that has just widened its licence has better near-term reasons to grow installs than to charge for them. The pressure argued here is structural rather than scheduled, and a structural pressure can be absorbed for a long time. The second is that the relicence pays for itself without any of this: Apache-2.0 widens who can adopt the runtime immediately, and a project can sit permissively licensed and unmonetised indefinitely. Plenty do.

The honest failure mode is quieter than either objection. The paid layer may arrive bundled inside a hosted product with its own name, priced as a whole rather than as a tier sitting above the runtime, in which case a reader looking for a pricing page next to a licence file will not find one and will call this wrong when it was right. The claim is about a price appearing on the layer above the runtime, not about the shape of the page it appears on.

reasoning.because: Herdr relicensed its runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0 in the same post that named its paid features
reasoning.given: AGPL's network-use clause was what reserved the hosted layer; Apache-2.0 gives that away
reasoning.so_that: Herdr publishes a price for the multi-machine and non-terminal features the post named as commercial
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a published price on a plan page, not a restated intent
reasoning.plain_language: Herdr just made its main tool free for anyone to reuse, so the money now has to come from paid extras.

summary: Herdr joined Y Combinator's F26 batch and, in the same post, relicensed its terminal agent runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0, naming multi-machine connectivity and non-terminal clients as the commercial layer. No funding figure was given. Expect a published price for that layer by Q2 2027.
